By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Two lives, one question: when suffering becomes unbearable, who gets to decide how it ends?

Unique Selling Point:
This story goes beyond the courtroom to reveal the deeply human stakes of assisted dying, through two people whose lived experiences led them to opposite conclusions. As a landmark legal battle unfolds, it captures a country at a moral crossroads - where dignity, choice and the value of life itself are fiercely contested.

Summary:
South Africa’s debate over medically assisted dying has unfolded over decades, shaped by a patchwork of legal precedent, constitutional principles, and unresolved moral questions. Under common law, assisted dying remains prohibited, reinforced by earlier rulings such as Hartman (1975) and Davison (2018). The South African Law Commission considered the issue in 1998, acknowledging its ethical complexity but the law was left unchanged.

The debate sharpened with the landmark Stransham-Ford v Minister of Justice and Correctional Services in 2015, where the High Court initially found that a terminally ill man should have the right to assisted dying, grounded in dignity and autonomy. That ruling was later overturned by the Supreme Court of Appeal on procedural grounds, leaving the constitutional question unresolved....and setting the stage for the current legal challenge.

Now, a fresh case seeks to directly test whether South Africa’s blanket ban is compatible with the Constitution of South Africa, particularly the rights to dignity, bodily integrity, and freedom from inhuman or degrading treatment. It is a case that could force the courts, and ultimately Parliament, to confront whether the right to life includes the right to choose one’s death.

At the heart of this legal battle are deeply personal stories that reflect the opposing sides of the argument. Dieter Harck, living with motor neurone disease, represents those who argue for autonomy. He is facing a progressive loss of control of his bodily functions and speech, and wants the legal right to decide how and when his life should end. In contrast, Petra Burger, who survived a catastrophic car accident and now works in palliative care, embodies the opposing view. Petra has been paralysed since age 24, confined to a wheelchair. Once desperate to die, she now sees meaning in what happened to her and describes it as a "gift" and "divine intervention". She fears that legalising assisted dying in an unequal healthcare system could expose vulnerable patients to harm.

Together, their stories bring human urgency to a legal question that has lingered for decades: whether dignity is best protected by preserving life at all costs, or by allowing individuals the freedom to choose when enough is enough.

Further information:
At the centre of the court challenge is Professor Willem Landman, a bioethicist and founder of Dignity SA, who has spent more than a decade advocating for the legalisation of medically assisted dying. He argues that the current legal framework is unconstitutional, denying competent, suffering individuals the right to make deeply personal end-of-life decisions.

Opposing this view is Dr Liz Gwyther, a leading voice in palliative care, who maintains that assisted dying is both unnecessary and dangerous. She argues that with proper palliative care, suffering can be managed, and warns that legalisation in a context of inequality and limited healthcare resources could place vulnerable patients at risk of coercion or neglect.

As the courts weigh whether the Constitution can be interpreted to include a right to medically assisted dying, South Africa is forced to confront a profound question: should the law prioritise the preservation of life at all costs, or recognise the right to choose one’s death in the face of unbearable suffering?

Script:


NATSOUND Goed seun goed seun

UPSOUND Petra Burger: I always believed I was destined to be a mother.

VO 1 Petra Burger dreamed of marriage and having children. But, thirty years ago, that dream was abruptly destroyed.

UPSOUND Petra Burger: I was on my way to church, then a tyre burst on the car and I was in a quite a horrific accident.

VO 2 On her wedding day, she was trapped in the wreckage of a car for hours.

UPSOUND Petra Burger: I could see that the bottom half of my body was turned down and I was looking up, and I asked one of the paramedics, this is bad isn’t it? And he said yes it’s bad.

VO 3 Petra suffered a devastating spinal injury and needed an emergency hysterectomy. She would never walk again, nor would she ever have a baby.

CR What happened to your fiancé?

UPSOUND Petra Burger: He walked out on me and that was very hard. I was very lonely. Heartbroken.

VO 4 It took years, but despite the trauma and loss, Petra found love again. She married and is now a social worker.

UPSOUND Petra Burger: Today I can look back and I can say it was divine intervention. My life was taking a path it wasn’t supposed to take and it brought me back on the path of my life, what it was destined to be, meant to be.

VO 5 Believing an incident of such significant trauma was somehow meant to be is a response many would find difficult to comprehend. But, it's one that adds a complex layer to a long standing debate that’s found its way into our courts.

UPSOUND Prof Willem Landman: We argue that there are four constitutional rights in our constitution that support a right to medical assistance in dying.

VO 6 Willem Landman is the co-founder of an organisation called DignitySA. Last month, he filed court papers of over a thousand pages backed by expert testimony and case studies in favour of assisted dying.

UPSOUND Prof Willem Landman: We believe that the reigning law, the common law which puts a blanket prohibition on medical assistance in dying, considering it as murder, we believe that this standoff between the constitution, this tension between the constitution and the common law must be resolved.

LINK: DignitySA defines assisted dying as a medically assisted death in two scenarios - in the one scenario a patient self-administers medication provided by a doctor, in the other the doctor administers the medication that ends the patient’s life.

UPSOUND Prof Willem Landman: If you qualify you have to ask to be medically assisted in dying and you have to ask more than once. There has to be a time lapse between the two. You have to be given the opportunity to opt out, to change your mind. So, the detail will have to be worked out.

VO 7 DignitySA argues that Parliament must draw up a legal framework that allows for assisted dying within strict criteria and safeguards - as many other countries do.

CR Do you think that South Africa is very behind the curve in terms of not having resolved this debate yet?

UPSOUND Prof Willem Landman: You know, in many respects, South Africa is ahead of the game, in terms of our labour laws. We have the most progressive termination of pregnancy act. But, somehow the last right is denied to people who need it. And it’s not a big group of people. It’s a tiny minority of people who are unfortunate in that they die in that way.

VO 8 It’s not clear whether the Minister of Health or three other respondents will oppose the legal challenge.

VO 9 Despite having suffered life changing trauma herself, Petra makes no secret of how she believes they should respond.

UPSOUND Petra Burger: I remember times when I felt it was too much, but I never thought of asking for euthanasia or anything. But, the moment we open this gate of assisted suicide, there’s going to be people with emotional burdens, financial burdens, physical burdens that’s going to speak to the wrong person. There’s going to be a child with a parent with dementia that’s just going to decide this is too hard.

UPSOUND Prof Liz Gwyther: We believe that euthanasia is unnecessary, it’s extreme, it’s irreversible.

VO 10 Ahead of a possible court hearing, Professor Liz Gwyther has formed an organisation in opposition to DignitySA’s move. Having worked in palliative care for decades, she worries vulnerable people could be coerced into choosing death.

UPSOUND Prof Liz Gwyther: My concern is that if society and the government decide that it can be lawful to kill somebody, how many unnecessary premature deaths are there going to be?

VO 11 She says the focus should rather be on improving the quality of palliative care.

CR Why do we still hear of people screaming in unbearable pain at the end of their life?

UPSOUND Prof Gwyther: Well that is absolutely unacceptable. It should never be a reason for euthanasia that a person has unbearable pain. Because pain can be controlled and in something like cancer it can be completely eliminated that a person doesn’t have pain and doesn’t have serious side effects from their medication, so pain should not be the reason.

UPSOUND Prof Willem Landman: Whatever we do, whatever law we pass must be consistent with the Constitution. Palliative care and medical assistance in dying are not two opposite poles. I think we should see medical assistance in dying as the end point of palliative care.

VO 12 77 year old Dieter Harck is one of DignitySA’s case studies. He was diagnosed with motor neurone disease - a rare progressive neurodegenerative disorder - 13 years ago.

NATSOUND CR: This was a story that Carte Blanche did in 2018.

VO 13 We met him in 2018.

NATSOUND Dieter: “It is a human right to decide”

VO 14 Dieter’s speech and mobility have declined significantly since then.

VO 15 He lives with his partner, Lynne Grubb.

UPSOUND Lynne Grubb: His brain is perfect, there’s no problem with the brain. It’s just the message from the brain giving to the muscles to move, and the message just doesn’t go through or goes through very very slowly, sometimes not at all.

VO 16 Before his diagnosis, Dieter ran a business and was physically active.

UPSOUND Lynne Grubb: Can I show you his medals. That’s all the races that Dieter used to do..Pick ‘n Pay cycle tour.

VO 17 Now, even the simplest tasks are a struggle.

UPSOUND Lynne Grubb: He’s a very, very proud, dignified man, and the end stage is going to be that he’s not going to be able to move very much. Breathing becomes a problem. Swallowing becomes a problem. Even saliva. You choke, you drown. I think Dieter faces a nightmare. And the sad thing about that is that he knows that.

VO 18 Dieter considered medically assisted death the moment his diagnosis was confirmed.

UPSOUND Lynne Grubb: Every single doctor that we saw, he asked the same question, can you help me when I need it, I don’t want it now, but when I need it can you help me and they all said no.

UPSOUND Dieter Harck: When the time arrives that being dead is better than being alive, then I want that choice.

VO 19 For now, Dieter still enjoys life but the outcome he hopes for when the struggle becomes unbearable might remain out of reach. Even if DignitySA’s case succeeds, it could take years for the law to change. Landman, though, is determined to see it through.

UPSOUND Prof Landman: Unnecessary suffering is wrong, injustice is wrong and I see both working together in the denial of medical assistance in dying in South Africa. And that keeps me going because it’s just not right.
